ety.text: Inherited from Middle English wolf, from Old English wulf, ƿulf, from Proto-West Germanic *wulf, from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos. Doublet of lobo and lupus. Cognates Cognate with Scots wouf, North Frisian wulew, Saterland Frisian and German Low German Wulf, West Frisian, Alemannic German, and Dutch wolf, Bavarian bolf, bölf, Woif, Cimbrian and Mòcheno bolf, German Wolf, Luxembourgish Wollef, Vilamovian wuf, Yiddish וואָלף (volf), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk ulv, Faroese úlvur, Icelandic úlfur, Swedish ulf, ulv, Gothic 𐍅𐌿𐌻𐍆𐍃 (wulfs); also Irish…

senses.d: Canis lupus; the largest wild member of the canine subfamily.
Any of several related canines that resemble Canis lupus in appearance, especially those of the genus Canis.
A man who makes amorous advances to many women.
A wolf tone or wolf note.
ex: The soft violin solo was marred by persistent wolves.

senses.d: Any very ravenous, rapacious, or destructive person or thing; especially, want; starvation.
ex: They toiled hard to keep the wolf from the door.

senses.d: One of the destructive, and usually hairy, larvae of several species of beetles and grain moths.
A white worm which infests granaries, the larva of Nemapogon granella, a tineid moth.
An eating ulcer or sore. See lupus.
ex: If God should send a cancer upon thy face, or a wolf into thy side

senses.d: A willying machine, that uses willow twigs to cleanse wool.
To devour; to gobble; to eat (something) voraciously.
ex: "Here's these legal ferrets has got our Puddin' in their clutches, and here's us, spellbound with anguish, watchin' them wolfin' it."
After a wolfed burger dinner, I called the night number at Administrative Vice and inquired about known lesbian gathering places.

senses.d: To make amorous advances to many women; to hit on women; to cruise for sex.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French loup, from an old western dialectal variant lou of Old French leu and reformed analogically from the feminine louve from Latin lupus (“wolf”). Cognate with Italian lupo; Portuguese and Spanish lobo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūpum, from Latin lŭpum. Doublet of lupus and lovo.

Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷosder. Proto-Italic *lukʷos Osco-Umbrianbor.? Latin lupus Old Spanish lobo Spanish lobo Inherited from Old Spanish lobo, from Latin lupus. Doublet of lupus (“lupus”, a learned borrowing) and Lope (a proper name from Basque).

Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷosder. Proto-Italic *lukʷos Osco-Umbrianbor.? Latin lupus Old Galician-Portuguese lobo Portuguese lobo Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lobo, from Latin lupus (“wolf”), from an Oscan-Umbrian language, from Proto-Italic *lukʷos, metathesis of Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos.
